lessons.title: Measurements and Units — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This self-tutoring lesson follows the JAMB Physics syllabus scope for Measurements and Units. Study the ideas in this order: identify the physical quantity or phenomenon, understand the governing law, learn the SI units and symbols, then practise interpretation and calculation. Do not memorise an equation without knowing what every symbol means and what conditions make the equation valid.

Syllabus coverage

length, area and volume measurements; metre rule; vernier calipers; micrometer screw-gauge; measuring cylinder; mass and beam balance; time; fundamental and derived quantities; dimensions; accuracy, errors, significant figures, standard form; position, distance, displacement, coordinates and frame of reference

Learning objectives

  • Explain the main ideas in Measurements and Units in your own words.
  • Identify the relevant physical law, definition, unit or equation before solving a problem.
  • Substitute numerical values carefully and keep units consistent.
  • Interpret graphs, physical situations and experimental observations where applicable.
  • Check whether the final answer is physically reasonable before accepting it.

How to study

  1. Read the overview and syllabus coverage slowly.
  2. Write down every important definition, SI unit and equation in a notebook.
  3. Work through the worked examples yourself before reading the explanation.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. For every wrong answer, identify the law or definition that should have been used and retry it.

Worked examples

Example 1: Which SI unit is used for length?

Solution: metre

Why: The SI base unit of length is the metre.

Example 2: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the diameter of a thin wire accurately?

Solution: micrometer screw-gauge

Why: A micrometer screw-gauge is designed for small dimensions such as wire diameter.

Example 3: Which instrument measures internal or external dimensions more precisely than a metre rule?

Solution: vernier calipers

Why: Vernier calipers provide finer readings than a metre rule.

Example 4: What is the SI unit of mass?

Solution: kilogram

Why: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram.

Example 5: Which quantity is a fundamental SI quantity?

Solution: time

Why: Time is fundamental; force, density and pressure are derived.

Example 6: What is the SI unit of force?

Solution: newton

Why: Force is a derived quantity measured in newtons.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an option because it sounds familiar without identifying the governing Physics principle.
  • Using a formula without checking the units, sign convention or stated conditions.
  • Confusing related quantities such as speed and velocity, mass and weight, or heat and temperature.
  • Rounding too early in numerical calculations and losing accuracy.
  • Ignoring diagrams, graph gradients, graph areas or direction information when they are part of the problem.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain Measurements and Units, identify the relevant law or equation, solve a new problem step by step, state the unit of the answer where appropriate, and justify why your chosen answer is correct.

lessons.html:
This self-tutoring lesson follows the JAMB Physics syllabus scope for Scalars and Vectors. Study the ideas in this order: identify the physical quantity or phenomenon, understand the governing law, learn the SI units and symbols, then practise interpretation and calculation. Do not memorise an equation without knowing what every symbol means and what conditions make the equation valid.

Syllabus coverage

scalar and vector quantities; examples; relative velocity; vector addition; resolution into perpendicular components; graphical methods

Learning objectives

  • Explain the main ideas in Scalars and Vectors in your own words.
  • Identify the relevant physical law, definition, unit or equation before solving a problem.
  • Substitute numerical values carefully and keep units consistent.
  • Interpret graphs, physical situations and experimental observations where applicable.

How to study

  1. Read the overview and syllabus coverage slowly.

  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. For every wrong answer, identify the law or definition that should have been used and retry it.

Worked examples

Example 1: Which quantity is a scalar?

Solution: speed

Why: Speed has magnitude only.

Example 2: Which quantity is a vector?

Solution: velocity

Why: Velocity has magnitude and direction.

Example 3: The resultant of two perpendicular vectors of 3 N and 4 N is

Solution: 5 N

Why: Using Pythagoras, R = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 N.

Example 4: Relative velocity of A with respect to B is represented by

Solution: vA - vB

Why: Relative velocity is the velocity of A measured from B.

Example 5: A vector resolved along perpendicular axes has

Solution: two rectangular components

Why: A planar vector can be resolved into perpendicular components.

Example 6: The resultant of equal and opposite vectors is

Solution: zero

Why: Equal and opposite vectors cancel.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an option because it sounds familiar without identifying the governing Physics principle.
  • Using a formula without checking the units, sign convention or stated conditions.
  • Confusing related quantities such as speed and velocity, mass and weight, or heat and temperature.
  • Rounding too early in numerical calculations and losing accuracy.
  • Ignoring diagrams, graph gradients, graph areas or direction information when they are part of the problem.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain Scalars and Vectors, identify the relevant law or equation, solve a new problem step by step, state the unit of the answer where appropriate, and justify why your chosen answer is correct.

Syllabus coverage

types of motion; relative motion; forces; speed, velocity and acceleration; equations of uniformly accelerated motion; motion under gravity; motion graphs; projectiles; Newton's laws; impulse and momentum; circular motion; simple harmonic motion; resonance

Learning objectives

  • Explain the main ideas in Motion in your own words.
  • Identify the relevant physical law, definition, unit or equation before solving a problem.

  5. For every wrong answer, identify the law or definition that should have been used and retry it.

Worked examples

Example 1: The slope of a distance-time graph represents

Solution: speed

Why: The gradient of distance against time is speed.

Example 2: The slope of a velocity-time graph represents

Solution: acceleration

Why: Acceleration is change of velocity per unit time.

Example 3: The area under a velocity-time graph gives

Solution: displacement

Why: Velocity multiplied by time gives displacement.

Example 4: Newton's second law relates force to

Solution: mass and acceleration

Why: For constant mass, F = ma.

Example 5: Linear momentum is given by

Solution: mv

Why: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity.

Example 6: For uniform circular motion, centripetal acceleration is directed

Solution: towards the centre

Why: Centripetal acceleration points toward the centre.

  • Choosing an option because it sounds familiar without identifying the governing Physics principle.
  • Using a formula without checking the units, sign convention or stated conditions.
  • Confusing related quantities such as speed and velocity, mass and weight, or heat and temperature.

lessons.html:
This self-tutoring lesson follows the JAMB Physics syllabus scope for Gravitational Field. Study the ideas in this order: identify the physical quantity or phenomenon, understand the governing law, learn the SI units and symbols, then practise interpretation and calculation. Do not memorise an equation without knowing what every symbol means and what conditions make the equation valid.

Syllabus coverage

Newton's law of universal gravitation; gravitational potential; conservative fields; acceleration due to gravity and variation of g; mass and weight; escape velocity; parking orbit and weightlessness

Learning objectives

  • Explain the main ideas in Gravitational Field in your own words.
  • Identify the relevant physical law, definition, unit or equation before solving a problem.
  • Substitute numerical values carefully and keep units consistent.
  • Interpret graphs, physical situations and experimental observations where applicable.
  • Check whether the final answer is physically reasonable before accepting it.

How to study

  1. Read the overview and syllabus coverage slowly.
  2. Write down every important definition, SI unit and equation in a notebook.
  3. Work through the worked examples yourself before reading the explanation.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. For every wrong answer, identify the law or definition that should have been used and retry it.

Worked examples

Example 1: Newton's law of gravitation states that gravitational force varies inversely with

Solution: the square of separation

Why: F is proportional to 1/r^2.

Example 2: Weight of a body is

Solution: mg

Why: Weight is the gravitational force on mass m.

Example 3: Gravitational field strength near a mass is defined as

Solution: force per unit mass

Why: Field strength is force experienced per unit mass.

Example 4: The SI unit of gravitational potential is

Solution: joule per kilogram

Why: Potential is gravitational potential energy per unit mass.

Example 5: Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to

Solution: leave a gravitational field without further propulsion

Why: It is the minimum launch speed for escape.

Example 6: A satellite in orbit is weightless because it is

Solution: in continuous free fall

Why: Orbital motion is continuous free fall under gravity.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an option because it sounds familiar without identifying the governing Physics principle.
  • Using a formula without checking the units, sign convention or stated conditions.
  • Confusing related quantities such as speed and velocity, mass and weight, or heat and temperature.
  • Rounding too early in numerical calculations and losing accuracy.
  • Ignoring diagrams, graph gradients, graph areas or direction information when they are part of the problem.

Self-test checkpoint

lessons.html:
This self-tutoring lesson follows the JAMB Physics syllabus scope for Equilibrium of Forces. Study the ideas in this order: identify the physical quantity or phenomenon, understand the governing law, learn the SI units and symbols, then practise interpretation and calculation. Do not memorise an equation without knowing what every symbol means and what conditions make the equation valid.

Syllabus coverage

equilibrium of coplanar forces; triangle and polygon of forces; Lami's theorem; moments; couples and torque; equilibrium of rigid bodies; resolution and composition of forces; resultant and equilibrant; centre of gravity; stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium

Learning objectives

  • Explain the main ideas in Equilibrium of Forces in your own words.
  • Identify the relevant physical law, definition, unit or equation before solving a problem.
  • Substitute numerical values carefully and keep units consistent.
  • Interpret graphs, physical situations and experimental observations where applicable.
  • Check whether the final answer is physically reasonable before accepting it.

How to study

  1. Read the overview and syllabus coverage slowly.
  2. Write down every important definition, SI unit and equation in a notebook.
  3. Work through the worked examples yourself before reading the explanation.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. For every wrong answer, identify the law or definition that should have been used and retry it.

Worked examples

Example 1: For a particle in equilibrium, the vector sum of forces is

Solution: zero

Why: Equilibrium requires zero resultant force.

Example 2: The moment of a force about a point equals

Solution: force x perpendicular distance

Why: Torque is force times perpendicular distance.

Example 3: A couple consists of

Solution: two equal, opposite and parallel forces separated by a distance

Why: A couple produces a turning effect without a resultant force.

Example 4: Lami's theorem applies to

Solution: three concurrent forces in equilibrium

Why: Lami's theorem relates three concurrent equilibrium forces.

Example 5: A stable equilibrium tends to

Solution: return to its original position after a small displacement

Why: A stable body returns after a small displacement.

Example 6: The equilibrant is

Solution: equal and opposite to the resultant

Why: The equilibrant cancels the resultant.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an option because it sounds familiar without identifying the governing Physics principle.
  • Using a formula without checking the units, sign convention or stated conditions.
  • Confusing related quantities such as speed and velocity, mass and weight, or heat and temperature.
  • Rounding too early in numerical calculations and losing accuracy.
  • Ignoring diagrams, graph gradients, graph areas or direction information when they are part of the problem.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain Equilibrium of Forces, identify the relevant law or equation, solve a new problem step by step, state the unit of the answer where appropriate, and justify why your chosen answer is correct.

This self-tutoring lesson follows the JAMB Physics syllabus scope for Work, Energy and Power. Study the ideas in this order: identify the physical quantity or phenomenon, understand the governing law, learn the SI units and symbols, then practise interpretation and calculation. Do not memorise an equation without knowing what every symbol means and what conditions make the equation valid.

Syllabus coverage

work, energy and power; forms of energy; conservation of energy; force-distance graphs; renewable and non-renewable energy; environmental impact; energy conversion; hydroelectric, nuclear and solar energy

Learning objectives

  • Explain the main ideas in Work, Energy and Power in your own words.
  • Identify the relevant physical law, definition, unit or equation before solving a problem.

  • Interpret graphs, physical situations and experimental observations where applicable.

  5. For every wrong answer, identify the law or definition that should have been used and retry it.

Worked examples

Example 1: Work done by a constant force is

Solution: Fs cos theta

Why: Only the force component along displacement does work.

Example 2: The SI unit of energy is

Solution: joule

Why: Energy is measured in joules.

Example 3: Power is the rate of

Solution: doing work

Why: Power is work done per unit time.

Example 4: Kinetic energy is

Solution: 1/2 mv^2

Why: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed squared.

Example 5: Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is

Solution: mgh

Why: Near the surface, gravitational potential energy is mgh.

Example 6: The principle of conservation of energy states that energy

Solution: cannot be created or destroyed but can be transformed

Why: Total energy is conserved in an isolated system.

  • Choosing an option because it sounds familiar without identifying the governing Physics principle.
  • Using a formula without checking the units, sign convention or stated conditions.
  • Confusing related quantities such as speed and velocity, mass and weight, or heat and temperature.

  • Ignoring diagrams, graph gradients, graph areas or direction information when they are part of the problem.

Worked examples

Example 1: Static friction acts when surfaces

Solution: are in contact without relative sliding

Why: Static friction prevents the onset of sliding.

Example 2: Limiting friction is the

Solution: maximum static friction just before motion begins

Why: It is the maximum value of static friction.

Example 3: Coefficient of friction is

Solution: limiting friction divided by normal reaction

Why: mu = F/R for limiting friction.

Example 4: One advantage of friction is that it

Solution: allows walking without slipping

Why: Friction provides grip.

Example 5: One method of reducing friction between machine parts is

Solution: lubrication

Why: Lubricants reduce direct surface contact.

Example 6: Stokes' law gives viscous drag on a small sphere as proportional to

Solution: radius x viscosity x speed

Why: Stokes' law is F = 6 pi eta r v.

Solution: load / effort

Example 2: Velocity ratio is

Solution: distance moved by effort / distance moved by load

Example 3: Efficiency of a machine is

Why: Efficiency compares useful output to input.

Example 4: A lever is a machine that uses

Solution: a rigid bar turning about a pivot

Why: A lever rotates about a fulcrum.

Example 5: An ideal machine has efficiency of

Solution: 100%

Why: An ideal machine has no energy losses.

Example 6: A pulley can be used to

Solution: change the direction or magnitude of an applied effort

Why: Pulley systems provide mechanical advantage and/or direction change.

Worked examples

Example 1: Hooke's law states that, within the elastic limit, extension is

Solution: proportional to force

Why: F is proportional to extension within the elastic limit.

Example 2: Young's modulus is

Solution: stress / strain

Why: Young's modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain.

Example 3: Elastic limit is the point beyond which a material

Solution: does not fully return to its original shape

Why: Beyond the elastic limit permanent deformation occurs.

Example 4: A spring balance measures

Solution: force

Why: A calibrated spring measures force.

Example 5: Elastic potential energy in a stretched spring is

Solution: 1/2 kx^2

Why: The work stored in a Hookean spring is 1/2 kx^2.

Example 6: Strain is

Solution: extension divided by original length

Why: Strain is a dimensionless ratio.

Solution: rho gh

Why: Gauge pressure due to a liquid column is rho gh.

Solution: atmospheric pressure

Why: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.

Example 5: Pascal's principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is

Solution: transmitted equally in all directions

Why: Pressure is transmitted through an enclosed fluid.

Example 6: Atmospheric pressure generally

Solution: decreases with altitude

Why: Air becomes less dense at greater altitude.

Worked examples

Example 1: Density is

Solution: mass per unit volume

Why: Density = m/V.

Example 2: Relative density is

Solution: density of substance divided by density of water

Why: Relative density is a ratio and has no unit.

Example 3: Upthrust on an immersed body equals

Solution: weight of fluid displaced

Why: This is Archimedes' principle.

Example 4: A floating body displaces liquid whose weight is

Solution: equal to the body's weight

Why: For equilibrium while floating, upthrust equals weight.

Example 5: A hydrometer measures

Solution: relative density of liquids

Why: Hydrometers are calibrated for liquid density/relative density.

Example 6: A body sinks when its average density is

Solution: greater than the liquid density

Why: A denser body experiences insufficient upthrust to float.

  • Choosing an option because it sounds familiar without identifying the governing Physics principle.
  • Using a formula without checking the units, sign convention or stated conditions.
  • Confusing related quantities such as speed and velocity, mass and weight, or heat and temperature.

Worked examples

Example 1: Heat is energy transferred because of a difference in

Solution: temperature

Why: Heat flows due to temperature difference.

Example 2: Heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of a body by

Solution: 1 K

Why: Heat capacity is heat per unit temperature rise.

Example 3: Specific heat capacity is heat required to raise the temperature of

Solution: unit mass by 1 K

Why: c is heat per unit mass per kelvin.

Example 4: The heat equation for sensible heating is

Solution: Q = mcΔT

Why: Q equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change.

Example 5: The method of mixtures is based mainly on

Solution: heat lost equals heat gained

Why: In an insulated mixture, heat exchanged balances.

Example 6: Newton's law of cooling says cooling rate is approximately proportional to

Solution: temperature excess over surroundings

Why: For modest temperature differences, cooling rate follows temperature excess.

Solution: without temperature change

Example 2: Specific latent heat of fusion concerns

Example 3: Specific latent heat of vaporisation concerns

Solution: liquid-gas change

Why: Vaporisation changes liquid to gas.

Solution: at the surface of a liquid

Why: Evaporation is a surface process and can occur below boiling point.

Example 5: Boiling occurs

Solution: throughout the liquid at its boiling point

Why: Boiling involves bubble formation throughout the liquid.

Example 6: Increasing pressure generally makes a liquid's boiling point

Solution: increase

Why: Higher pressure requires higher temperature for vapour pressure to match it.

Solution: frequency

Example 2: Loudness is related mainly to

Solution: intensity of sound

Why: This is the stated fundamental relation for a stretched string.

Solution: approximately twice the pipe length

Why: An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, giving λ ≈ 2L.

Why: Resonance produces large amplitude when driving frequency matches a natural frequency.

Example 6: Linear magnification is

Solution: image height divided by object height

Why: Magnification compares image and object heights.

Worked examples

Example 1: A semiconductor has conductivity

Solution: between that of a conductor and an insulator

Why: Semiconductors have intermediate conductivity.

Example 2: An intrinsic semiconductor is

Solution: chemically pure semiconductor material

Why: Intrinsic material has no intentional impurity doping.

Example 3: An n-type semiconductor has majority carriers that are

Solution: electrons

Why: Donor impurities provide extra electrons.

Example 4: A p-type semiconductor has majority carriers that are

Solution: holes

Why: Acceptor impurities create holes as majority carriers.

Example 5: A diode is commonly used for

Solution: rectification

Why: A diode allows preferential current in one direction.

Example 6: A transistor can be used for

Solution: amplification

Why: Transistors can amplify electrical signals.
